## Discussion

A muscle model is deﬁned by the experiments it can replicate and the mechanisms it embodies. We have developed the VEXAT muscle model to replicate the force response of muscle to a wide variety of perturbations (Kirsch et al., 1994; Herzog and Leonard, 2002; Leonard et al., 2010) while also retaining the ability to reproduce the force-velocity experiment of Hill, 1938 and the force-length experiment of Gordon et al., 1966. The model we have developed uses two mechanisms to capture the force response of muscle over a large variety of time and length scales: ﬁrst, a viscoelastic crossbridge element that over brief time-scales appears as a spring-damper, and at longer time-scales mimics a Hill-model; second, a titin element that is capable of developing active force during large stretches.

The viscoelastic crossbridge and titin elements we have developed introduce a number of assumptions into the model. While there is evidence that the activation-dependent stiffness of muscle originates primarily from the stiffness of the attached crossbridges (Veigel et al., 1998), the origins of the activation-dependent damping observed by Kirsch et al., 1994 have not yet been established. We assumed that, since the damping observed by Kirsch et al., 1994 varies linearly with activation, the damping originates from the attached crossbridges. Whether this damping is intrinsic or is due to some other factor remains to be established. Next, we have also assumed that the force developed by the XE converges to a Hill model (Millard et al., 2013) given enough time (Equation 16). A recent experiment (see Figure 7 of Tomalka et al., 2021) suggests the force developed by the XE might decrease during lengthening rather than increasing as is typical of a Hill model (Millard et al., 2013). If the observations of Tomalka et al., 2021 can be replicated, the VEXAT model will need to be adjusted so that the XE element develops less force during active lengthening while the active-titin element develops more force. Finally, we have assumed that actin-myosin sliding acceleration (due to crossbridge cycling) occurs when there is a force imbalance between the external force applied to the XE and the internal force developed by the XE as shown in Equation 16. This assumption is a departure from previous models: Hill-type models (Zajac, 1989; Millard et al., 2013) assume that the tension applied to the muscle instantaneously affects the actin-myosin sliding velocity; Huxley models (Huxley, 1957) assume that the actin-myosin sliding velocity directly affects the rate of attachment and detachment of crossbridges.

The active titin model that we have developed makes assumptions similar to Rode et al., 2009 and Schappacher-Tilp et al., 2015: some parts of the PEVK segment bond to actin, and this bond cannot do any positive work on titin. The assumption that the bond between titin and actin cannot do positive work means that titin cannot be actively preloaded: it can only develop force when it is stretched. In contrast, two mechanisms have been proposed that make it possible for titin to be preloaded by crossbridge cycling: the winding ﬁlament theory of Nishikawa et al., 2012 and the titin entanglement hypothesis of DuVall et al., 2016. If titin were signiﬁcantly preloaded by crossbridge cycling, the titin load path would support higher forces and the myosin-actin load path would bear less force. Accordingly, the overall stiffness of the CE would be reduced, affecting our simulations of Kirsch et al., 1994: lower myosin-actin loads mean fewer attached crossbridges, since crossbridges are stiff in comparison to titin, the stiffness of the CE would decrease (see Appendix 1). Hopefully experimental work will clarify if titin can be actively preloaded by crossbridges in the future.

Both the viscoelastic crossbridge and active titin elements include simple myosin-actin and titin-actin bond models that improve accuracy but have limitations. First, the viscoelastic crossbridge element has been made to represent a population of crossbridges in which the contribution of any single crossbridge is negligible. Although it may be possible for the XE model to accurately simulate a maximally activated single sarcomere (which has roughly 20 attached crossbridges per half sarcomere Huxley and Simmons, 1971; Howard, 1997), the accuracy of the model will degrade as the number of attached crossbridges decreases. When only a single crossbridge remains, the XE model’s output will be inaccurate because it can only generate force continuously while a real crossbridge generates force discretely each time it attaches to, and detaches from, actin. Next, we have used two equations, Equation 16 and Equation 21, that assume myosin-actin and titin-actin interactions are temperature-invariant and scale linearly with size ($l_{o}^{M}$ and $f_{o}^{M}$). In contrast, myosin-actin interactions and some titin-actin interactions are temperature-sensitive (Minajeva et al., 2002; Roots et al., 2012) and may not scale linearly with size. In the ‘Active lengthening beyond actin-myosin overlap’ section we had to adjust the active titin damping parameter, $\beta_{A}^{PEVK}$, to simulate the myoﬁbril experiments of Leonard et al., 2010, perhaps because the assumptions of temperature-invariance and size-linearity were not met: the initial value for $\beta_{A}^{PEVK}$ came from ﬁtting to in-situ experimental data (Herzog and Leonard, 2002) from whole muscle that was warmer (35 − 36.5°C vs 20 − 21°C) and larger ($l_{o}^{M}$ of 42.9mm vs. 10 − 15μm) than the myoﬁbrils (Leonard et al., 2010). While the cat soleus XE and titin model parameters (Table 1G, H1) can be used as rough default values, these parameters should be reﬁt to accurately simulate muscle that differs in scale or temperature from cat soleus. Finally, the VEXAT model in its current form ignores phenomena related to submaximal contractions: the shift in the peak of the force-length relation (Stephenson and Wendt, 1984), and the scaling of the maximum shortening velocity (Chow and Darling, 1999). We hope to include these phenomena in a later version of the VEXAT model to more accurately simulate submaximal contractions.

The model we have proposed can replicate phenomena that occur at a wide variety of time and length scales: the experiments of Kirsch et al., 1994 which occur over small time and length scales; and the active lengthening experiments of Herzog and Leonard, 2002 and Leonard et al., 2010 which occur over physiological and supra-physiological length scales. In contrast, we have shown in the ‘Biological benchmark simulations’ section that a Hill-type model compares poorly to biological muscle when the same set of experiments are simulated. We expect that a Huxley model (Huxley, 1957) is also likely to have difficulty reproducing the experiment of Kirsch et al., 1994 because the model lacks an active damping element. Since titin was discovered (Maruyama, 1976) long after Huxley’s model was proposed (Huxley, 1957), a Huxley model will be unable to replicate any experiment that is strongly inﬂuenced by titin such as the experiment of Leonard et al., 2010.

Although there have been several more recent muscle model formulations proposed, none have the properties to simultaneously reproduce the experiments of Kirsch et al., 1994, Herzog and Leonard, 2002, Leonard et al., 2010, Hill, 1938, and Gordon et al., 1966. Linearized impedance models (Hogan, 1985; Mussa-Ivaldi et al., 1985) can reproduce the experiments of Kirsch et al., 1994, but these models lack the nonlinear components needed to reproduce the force-length experiments of Gordon et al., 1966, and the force-velocity experiments of Hill, 1938. The models of Forcinito et al., 1998, and Tahir et al., 2018 have a structure that places a contractile element in series with an elastic-tendon. While this is a commonly used structure, at high frequencies the lack of damping in the tendon will drive the phase shift between length and force to approach zero. The measurements and model of Kirsch et al., 1994, in contrast, indicate that the phase shift between length and force approaches ninety degrees with increasing frequencies. Although the Hill-type models of Haeufle et al., 2014 and Günther et al., 2018 have viscoelastic tendons, these models have no representation of the viscoelasticity of the CE’s attached crossbridges. Similar to the Hill-type muscle model evaluated in this work (Millard et al., 2013), it is likely that models of Haeufle et al., 2014 and Günther et al., 2018 will not be able to match the frequency response of biological muscle. While the model of Tamura and Saito, 2002 is one of the few models that can develop force-enhancement and force-depression (Tamura et al., 2005), it is unlikely that this model will be able to reproduce the frequency response of biological muscle because it uses spring-damping elements in series: Kirsch et al., 1994 showed that the frequency response of spring-damping elements in series poorly fits the response of biological muscle. The models of De Groote et al., 2017 and De Groote et al., 2018 introduced a short-range-stiffness element in parallel to a Hill model to capture the stiffness of biological muscle. While the formulations presented in De Groote et al., 2017 and De Groote et al., 2018 improves upon a Hill model it is unlikely to reproduce the experiement of Kirsch et al., 1994 because we have shown in the ‘Active lengthening beyond actin-myosin overlap’ section that a Hill model has a frequency response that differs from biological muscle. The muscle model of Rode et al., 2009 uses a Hill model for the CE and so we expect that this model will have the same difficulties reproducing the experiment of Kirsch et al., 1994. The model of Schappacher-Tilp et al., 2015 extends a Huxley model (Huxley, 1957) by adding a detailed titin element. Similar to a Huxley model, the model of Schappacher-Tilp et al., 2015 will likely have difficulty reproducing the experiment of Kirsch et al., 1994 because it is missing an active damping element.

While developing this model, we have come across open questions that we hope can be addressed in the future. How does muscle stiffness and damping change across the force-length curve? Does stiffness and damping change with velocity? What are the physical origins of the active damping observed by Kirsch et al., 1994? What are the conditions that affect passive-force enhancement, and its release? In addition to pursuing these questions, we hope that other researchers continue to contribute experiments that are amenable to simulation, and to develop musculotendon models that overcome the limitations of our model. To help others build upon our work, we have made the source code of the model and all simulations presented in this paper available online (see the elife 2023 branch of https://github.com/mjhmilla/Millard2021ImpedanceMuscle; copy archived at Millard, 2024).

Muscle models are important tools in the fields of biomechanics and physiology. Muscle models serve a wide variety of functions, including validating existing theories, testing new hypotheses, and predicting forces produced by humans and animals in health and disease. This paper attempts to provide an alternative to Hill-type muscle models that includes contributions of titin to force enhancement over multiple time scales. Due to the significant limitations of Hill-type models, alternative models are needed and therefore the work is important and timely.

The effort to include a role for titin in muscle models is a major strength of the methods and results. The results clearly demonstrate the weaknesses of Hill models and the advantages of incorporating titin into theoretical treatments of muscle mechanics. Another strength is to address muscle mechanics over a large range of time scales.

The authors succeed in demonstrating the need to incorporate titin in muscle models, and further show that the model accurately predicts in situ force of cat soleus (Kirsch et al. 1994; Herzog & Leonard, 2002) and rabbit posts myofibrils (Leonard et al. 2010). However, it remains unclear whether the model will be practical for use with data from different muscles or preparations. Several ad hoc modifications were described in the paper, and the degree to which the model requires parameter optimization for different muscles, preparations and experiment types remains unclear.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.88344.4.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.88344.4.sa2)

This model of skeletal muscle includes springs and dampers which aim to capture the effect of crossbridge and titin stiffness during the stretch of active muscle. While both crossbridge and titin stiffness have previously been incorporated, in some form, into models, this model is the first to simultaneously include both. The authors suggest that this will allow for the prediction of muscle force in response to short-, mid- and long-range stretches. All these types of stretch are likely to be experienced by muscle during in vivo perturbations, and are known to elicit different muscle responses. Hence, it is valuable to have a single model which can predict muscle force under all these physiologically relevant conditions. In addition, this model dramatically simplifies sarcomere structure to enable this muscle model to be used in multi-muscle simulations of whole-body movement.

In order to test this model, its force predictions are compared to 3 sets of experimental data which focus on short-, mid- and long-range perturbations, and to the predictions of a Hill-type muscle model. The choice of data sets is excellent and provide a robust test of the model's ability to predict forces over a range of length perturbations. However, I find the comparison to a Hill-type muscle model to be somewhat limiting. It is well established that Hill-type models do not have any mechanism by which they can predict the effect of active muscle stretch. Hence, that the model proposed here represents an improvement over such a model is not a surprise. Many other models, some of which are also simple enough to be incorporated into whole-body simulations, have incorporated mechanistic elements which allow for the prediction of force responses to muscle stretch. And it is not clear from the results presented here that this model would outperform such models.

The paper begins by outlining the phenomenological vs mechanistic approaches taken to muscle modelling, historically. It appears, although is not directly specified, that this model combines these approaches. A somewhat mechanistic model of the response of the crossbridges and titin to active stretch is combined with a phenomenological implementation of force-length and force-velocity relationships. This combination of approaches may be useful improving the accuracy of predictions of muscle models and whole-body simulations, which is certainly a worthy goal. However, it also may limit the insight that can be gained. For example, it does not seem that this model could reflect any effect of active titin properties on muscle shortening. In addition, it is not clear to me, either physiologically or in the model, what drives the shift from the high stiffness in short-range perturbations to the somewhat lower stiffness in mid-range perturbations.

results.result: The VEXAT model can replicate muscle response to length changes across multiple scales (small and large perturbations) while reproducing force-velocity and force-length relations, and is computationally efficient with few states.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9, C52-C53 collectively establish the main contribution of the paper. The model's performance is demonstrated through simulations of multiple benchmark experiments (Kirsch et al. 1994, Herzog and Leonard 2002, Leonard et al. 2010, Hill 1938, Gordon et al. 1966) shown in Figures 6-12, with quantitative comparisons to both biological data and Hill-type models. The computational efficiency claim (C53) is supported by the model's state count (4-5 states vs. thousands for Huxley models).

results.result: The VEXAT model achieves 89% VAF at 90 Hz perturbations (within the 78-99% range of Kirsch et al. 1994), outperforming the Hill model (58% VAF), though both models show greater phase shift than biological muscle at low frequencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 are directly supported by simulation data in Figure 6, comparing model outputs to Kirsch et al. 1994 experiments. The VAF values are quantitatively reported and compared to experimental benchmarks. The limitation regarding low-frequency phase response (C80) is acknowledged with visual evidence in Figure 6C, F, I, L.

results.result: In simulations of Herzog and Leonard 2002 active lengthening experiments, the VEXAT model develops steadily increasing tension while the Hill model exhibits force drops due to negative stiffness on the descending limb of the force-length curve.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 are supported by simulation results in Figure 9B-C, showing divergent behavior between models. The VEXAT model's continued force development is mechanistically explained by the titin model, while the Hill model's negative stiffness is shown both in simulation and explained mathematically (Equation 26). This addresses a key limitation of Hill-type models.

results.result: When simulating Leonard et al. 2010 experiments of active lengthening beyond actin-myosin overlap, only the VEXAT model with linear titin element matches experimental data, while the Hill model cannot produce force beyond 1.62 optimal length.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86, C89-C90 are supported by Figure 10B showing the VEXAT model (linear titin) matching experimental data up to 3.38 optimal length, while the Hill model fails beyond actin-myosin overlap. The titin-deletion control experiment (C89) from Leonard et al. 2010 provides mechanistic validation. However, the WLC titin model fails to reach observed lengths, suggesting model limitations at extreme extensions.

results.result: The VEXAT model has limitations: the low frequency phase response can be improved, and the model lacks a mechanism to support passive force enhancement.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 are acknowledged limitations supported by data in Figure 6C, F showing phase deviations at low frequencies, and Figure 9B showing the model fails to capture passive force enhancement (ΔfB) after deactivation. These are honest assessments of model shortcomings compared to biological muscle.

results.result: The VEXAT model's force-velocity curve shows slightly weaker maximum shortening velocity than the embedded curve due to XE viscoelasticity, and the force-length profile is right-shifted due to XE series elasticity, both correctable through calibration.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 are supported by Figure 11A and Figure 12A showing the deviations and their corrections. The mathematical basis for the shift (2/k̃ₒˣ) is derived in Equations 30-31. The calibration approach (scaling vₘₐₓᴹ by 0.95 and shifting fᴸ) successfully aligns the model with target curves.

results.result: Kirsch et al. 1994 demonstrated that muscle behaves as a linear-time-invariant system for small perturbations, with a spring-damper capturing >90% of force variation across 4-90 Hz, and damping increasing as perturbation bandwidth decreases.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17, C74, C76 accurately cite and describe the Kirsch et al. 1994 findings, which form a key experimental benchmark for the paper. These are well-established results in the literature used to validate the VEXAT model. The claims are consistent with the cited work and provide appropriate context.

results.result: The origins of activation-dependent damping observed by Kirsch et al. 1994 are unknown, but the VEXAT model assumes it originates from attached crossbridges since damping varies linearly with activation.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 correctly identifies an open question in the field. Claim C97 presents a modeling assumption based on the linear relationship between damping and activation, but this remains unvalidated. The assumption is reasonable but speculative, as acknowledged in the Discussion. This represents a hypothesis requiring future experimental validation.

results.result: Recent experiments (Tomalka et al. 2021) suggest the XE force might decrease during lengthening rather than increase, which would require model adjustments if replicated.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 identify a potential conflict between the VEXAT model and recent experimental observations. However, the authors appropriately note this requires replication before model revision. This represents responsible acknowledgment of potentially contradictory evidence, but the uncertainty about replicability prevents definitive evaluation.

results.result: Hill-type models lack active spring elements, Huxley models lack active damping, and linearized models cannot capture nonlinear force-velocity and force-length relations, limiting their ability to replicate the full range of muscle behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27, C109-C110 accurately characterize limitations of existing model classes based on their mathematical structure and cited literature. These are well-established properties of these model types. The inferences about their inability to replicate certain experiments (C109-C110) follow logically from their structural limitations.

results.result: Multiple existing muscle models (Forcinito et al. 1998, Tamura and Saito 2002, Haeufle et al. 2014, Günther et al. 2018, De Groote et al. 2017/2018, Rode et al. 2009, Schappacher-Tilp et al. 2015) are unlikely to reproduce Kirsch et al. 1994 experiments due to structural limitations (serial vs. parallel spring-damper arrangements, missing damping elements, or reliance on Hill-type CE).
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31, C111-C118 provide systematic analysis of why existing models cannot replicate the Kirsch et al. 1994 experiments. The reasoning is based on: (1) mathematical structure of the models from cited papers, (2) Kirsch et al. 1994's explicit demonstration that serial spring-dampers fail (C31), and (3) impedance properties of series vs. parallel connections. The inferences are logical and well-supported, though direct simulation comparisons would strengthen the argument.

results.result: Titin is a complex, multi-segmented protein spanning the half-sarcomere with variable composition across muscle types and species, capable of activation-dependent interactions with actin and myosin at multiple sites (N2A, PEVK, IgD regions).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C41, C64-C66 accurately summarize established knowledge about titin structure and interactions, supported by multiple citations to experimental work. These claims provide necessary biological context for the titin model development. The variety of reported interaction sites (C38-C41, C64-C66) reflects genuine complexity and uncertainty in the literature.

results.result: The VEXAT model assumes titin-actin interaction (rather than titin-myosin) based on weight of evidence, modeled as activation-dependent damping rather than rigid attachment, consistent with in vitro motility assays showing slowed but not stopped actin progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 present justified modeling choices based on experimental evidence. C67 acknowledges the weight of evidence favors titin-actin over titin-myosin interactions. C68-C69 justify the damping model based on Kellermayer and Granzier 1996 and Dutta et al. 2018 observations. These are reasonable modeling decisions given current evidence, though alternative mechanisms remain possible.

results.result: The VEXAT model treats actin and myosin filaments as rigid and lumps six titin filaments together to reduce computational states, justified by the much higher stiffness of actin/myosin filaments compared to crossbridges.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 present modeling simplifications with clear justification. C61 is supported by citations showing actin/myosin stiffness greatly exceeds crossbridge stiffness. C62-C63 explicitly state these as simplifying assumptions to reduce model complexity. The trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency is appropriate for the model's intended use in large-scale simulations.

results.result: The VEXAT model assumes actin-myosin sliding acceleration occurs due to force imbalance in the XE, departing from Hill models (instantaneous velocity response) and Huxley models (velocity-dependent attachment/detachment rates).
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 clearly articulate a key modeling assumption (C100) and contrast it with established approaches (C101-C102). The assumption is stated transparently with mathematical support (Equation 16). While this represents a novel approach, it remains a hypothesis requiring experimental validation. The departure from previous models is accurately characterized.

results.result: The VEXAT model's active titin assumes PEVK-actin bonds cannot do positive work on titin (similar to Rode et al. 2009 and Schappacher-Tilp et al. 2015), meaning titin cannot be actively preloaded and only develops force when stretched.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 clearly state a modeling assumption and its consequence. C105 explores implications if the assumption were violated (titin preloading would reduce CE stiffness). The assumption is acknowledged as differing from alternative theories (winding filament, titin entanglement). This represents an honest presentation of a modeling choice with uncertain biological validity.

results.result: The VEXAT model has limitations: inaccuracy with single crossbridges (lumped model assumption), temperature-invariance assumption (contradicting temperature-sensitive interactions), and ignoring submaximal contraction phenomena (force-length peak shift, velocity scaling).
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 honestly acknowledge model limitations. C106 correctly identifies the breakdown of the lumped crossbridge approach at low crossbridge numbers. C107 notes temperature-sensitivity (supported by citations) is not captured. C108 identifies missing submaximal contraction phenomena (supported by citations). These represent appropriate scope limitations for the current model version.

results.result: Mechanical properties scaling with size is commonly used in muscle modeling, and titin's passive force-length properties scale from single molecules to myofibrils.
results.evaluation: Claims C55 and C59 cite established scaling principles in muscle modeling. C55 is supported by Zajac 1989, a foundational reference. C59 is supported by Herzog et al. 2012 and Prado et al. 2005 showing titin scaling. These provide justification for the model's scaling assumptions and are well-established in the literature.

results.result: Muscle impedance (stiffness and damping) is fundamental to motor learning and stability, with small perturbations captured by LTI spring-damper systems and large stretches by compliant springs with activation-dependent fixing, relevant to locomotion and injury prediction.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide well-established background context supported by appropriate citations. These claims accurately summarize the functional importance of muscle mechanical properties and motivate the need for models capturing both small and large perturbations. The claims represent accepted knowledge in the field.

results.result: No single existing muscle model can replicate force responses to both small and large perturbations while reproducing Hill 1938 and Gordon et al. 1966 experiments, potentially leading simulation studies to reach conclusions valid in simulation but not reality.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C22-C23 identify the gap in existing models that motivates the VEXAT development. These are inferences based on the authors' analysis of existing model capabilities. While C23 is somewhat speculative about simulation study conclusions, the core claim about model limitations (C6, C22) is supported by the systematic analysis of existing models provided later in the paper.

results.result: The CNS exploits muscle impedance for motor learning, unstable/noisy environments, using co-contraction to increase arm stiffness in unstable force fields, with co-contraction reducing as tasks become learned.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C15 accurately cite and summarize motor control literature (Franklin et al. 2003, Trumbower et al. 2009, Selen et al. 2009, Burdet et al. 2001). These provide important functional context for why accurate impedance modeling matters. The claims represent well-established findings in motor control research.

results.result: Active muscle stretched appreciably develops enormous titin forces that may prevent injury, with stiffness for small perturbations far exceeding that for large perturbations, both relevant to everyday movements.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 provide context for the importance of modeling both small and large perturbations. C18 is supported by Herzog and Leonard 2002 and Leonard et al. 2010. C19 is speculative ("may prevent") but reasonable. C20 compares stiffness across scales (supported by comparing cited studies). C21 provides functional motivation. These establish the biological relevance of the modeling challenge.

results.result: The Sartori et al. 2015 approach of deriving stiffness from force-length curve slope predicts zero stiffness at optimal length and negative stiffness on descending limb, contradicting experimental evidence; De Groote et al. 2017/2018 short-range-stiffness model has sharp transitions and unchanged damping.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C51 provide critical analysis of recent attempts to add stiffness to Hill models. The mathematical inferences about Sartori et al. 2015 (C45-C46) are correct given the approach described. The contradictions with experimental data (C47-C48, supported by Kirsch et al. 1994 and Herzog and Leonard 2002) are valid. The critiques of De Groote et al. 2017/2018 (C49-C51) are supported by comparison with Kirsch et al. 1994 data.

results.result: The Forcinito et al. 1998 model more faithfully replicates force development during ramp length changes (≈10% optimal length, 4-11% max velocity) than Hill models; Tamura and Saito 2002 replicated force-length-velocity relations and qualitatively reproduced force-enhancement/depression profiles.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 accurately cite improvements in previous models. These claims provide appropriate credit to prior work while setting up the argument that these models still cannot replicate the full range of experiments (particularly Kirsch et al. 1994). The characterization of these models' capabilities is consistent with the cited literature.

results.result: Most motor control simulations use the canonical linearized muscle model.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 is supported by multiple citations to motor control simulation studies (Kearney et al. 1997, Perreault et al. 2004, Schouten et al. 2008, Trumbower et al. 2009, Mitrovic et al. 2010). This provides context for the practical importance of accurate impedance modeling in motor control applications.

results.result: The VEXAT model can replicate muscle responses to length changes across multiple scales (small and large perturbations), more accurately captures impedance and active lengthening responses than Hill-type models, and is computationally efficient with few states for large-scale simulations.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers affirm the model's value and performance. Reviewer 1 states 'the evidence presented to support the model is solid, since it outperforms Hill-type models in a variety of conditions.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the authors succeed in demonstrating the need to incorporate titin in muscle models' and confirms the model 'accurately predicts in situ force' from multiple experimental datasets. Reviewer 3 acknowledges the model 'is the first to simultaneously include both' crossbridge and titin stiffness.

results.result: The VEXAT model can reproduce classical force-velocity and force-length relations of muscle, though with slight differences from embedded curves due to series viscoelasticity and a rightward shift in the force-length profile.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these claims about the model's ability to reproduce classical muscle properties. Reviewer 2 explicitly states the model 'accurately predicts in situ force' from multiple datasets including those testing force-length and force-velocity relations. The acknowledged differences are presented as model characteristics rather than failures.

results.result: The VEXAT model has limitations including poor low-frequency phase response, inability to match experimental VAF at 15 Hz perturbations, greater phase shift than biological data at low frequencies, and lack of a mechanism for passive force enhancement.
results.evaluation: These limitations are acknowledged by the authors and not disputed by reviewers. Reviewer 1 notes 'the combination of phenomenological and mechanistic aspects of the model may sometimes make it challenging to interpret the output,' which relates to these limitations. Reviewer 3 states 'it is not clear to me, either physiologically or in the model, what drives the shift from the high stiffness in short-range perturbations to the somewhat lower stiffness in mid-range perturbations,' indicating unresolved mechanistic questions.

results.result: At 90 Hz perturbations, the VEXAT model achieves 89% VAF (within the experimental range of 78-99%), while the Hill model achieves only 58% VAF.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these comparative performance results. Reviewer 1 states 'the evidence presented to support the model is solid, since it outperforms Hill-type models in a variety of conditions.' Reviewer 2 confirms the model 'accurately predicts in situ force of cat soleus (Kirsch et al. 1994)' which includes these high-frequency perturbation experiments.

results.result: During active lengthening on the descending limb, the VEXAT model continues to develop tension while the Hill model's tension drops due to negative stiffness, demonstrating that biological muscle does not exhibit negative stiffness in this region.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this key advantage of the VEXAT model. Reviewer 1 notes the model 'outperforms Hill-type models in a variety of conditions.' Reviewer 2 states 'The results clearly demonstrate the weaknesses of Hill models and the advantages of incorporating titin into theoretical treatments of muscle mechanics.' This finding addresses a fundamental limitation of Hill-type models.

results.result: The Leonard et al. 2010 experiment shows active force continues to develop linearly during lengthening beyond actin-myosin overlap until mechanical failure, with titin-deleted myofibrils failing at short lengths and low stresses. Only the VEXAT model with linear titin element can match this experimental data.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these results. Reviewer 2 explicitly states the authors 'show that the model accurately predicts...rabbit psoas myofibrils (Leonard et al. 2010).' Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'The effort to include a role for titin in muscle models is a major strength of the methods and results' and that this addresses force responses to 'long-range stretches.'

results.result: Prior to this work, no single muscle model could replicate force responses to both small and large perturbations while reproducing classical Hill and Gordon experiments, potentially leading simulation studies to reach conclusions valid in simulation but not reality.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this gap in the literature. Reviewer 2 states 'Due to the significant limitations of Hill-type models, alternative models are needed and therefore the work is important and timely.' Reviewer 3 notes 'it is valuable to have a single model which can predict muscle force under all these physiologically relevant conditions,' confirming the previous absence of such a model.

results.result: Existing models have fundamental structural limitations: Hill models lack active spring elements, Huxley models lack active damping, linearized models cannot capture nonlinear relations, and several modified Hill models use serial rather than parallel spring-damper connections that fail to reproduce experimental phase shifts.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these characterizations of existing models. Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'It is well established that Hill-type models do not have any mechanism by which they can predict the effect of active muscle stretch,' confirming the structural limitations described. These claims provide context for the model development rather than novel findings.

results.result: The VEXAT model makes several simplifying assumptions: treating actin and myosin filaments as rigid, lumping six titin filaments together, assuming titin-actin rather than titin-myosin interaction, modeling this interaction as activation-dependent damping rather than rigid attachment, and assuming titin cannot be actively preloaded.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express concerns about the model's assumptions and their implications. Reviewer 2 states 'it remains unclear whether the model will be practical for use with data from different muscles or preparations. Several ad hoc modifications were described in the paper.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the combination of phenomenological and mechanistic aspects...may limit the insight that can be gained' and questions 'what drives the shift from the high stiffness in short-range perturbations to the somewhat lower stiffness in mid-range perturbations,' suggesting uncertainty about whether the assumptions capture the underlying physiology correctly.

results.result: While activation-dependent stiffness originates from crossbridges, the origins of activation-dependent damping are not yet established. The VEXAT model assumes damping originates from attached crossbridges because it varies linearly with activation.
results.evaluation: This assumption is not directly challenged but falls under broader reviewer concerns about mechanistic interpretation. Reviewer 3 states 'it is not clear to me, either physiologically or in the model, what drives the shift from the high stiffness in short-range perturbations to the somewhat lower stiffness,' indicating uncertainty about the physiological basis of model components including damping mechanisms.

results.result: Recent experiments (Tomalka et al. 2021) suggest crossbridge force might decrease during lengthening rather than increase as in Hill models, which would require adjusting the VEXAT model if replicated.
results.evaluation: This is presented as a speculative future modification. Reviewers do not comment on this specific claim, but Reviewer 2's concern that 'the degree to which the model requires parameter optimization for different muscles, preparations and experiment types remains unclear' suggests uncertainty about how the model would need to be adapted to accommodate new experimental findings.

results.result: The VEXAT model in its current form ignores phenomena related to submaximal contractions including the shift in peak force-length relation and scaling of maximum shortening velocity.
results.evaluation: This limitation is acknowledged by the authors and not disputed by reviewers. Reviewer 2 notes 'it remains unclear whether the model will be practical for use with data from different muscles or preparations,' which encompasses these unmodeled phenomena. This is treated as a known limitation rather than a fundamental flaw.

results.result: Various alternative models (Huxley, linearized impedance, Forcinito, Haeufle, Günther, Tamura, De Groote, Rode, Schappacher-Tilp) are predicted to have difficulty reproducing the Kirsch et al. 1994 experiment due to structural limitations such as lacking active damping, using serial connections, or missing titin components.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 directly challenges the limited comparison: 'I find the comparison to a Hill-type muscle model to be somewhat limiting...Many other models, some of which are also simple enough to be incorporated into whole-body simulations, have incorporated mechanistic elements which allow for the prediction of force responses to muscle stretch. And it is not clear from the results presented here that this model would outperform such models.' This indicates the predictions about other models' performance are not adequately demonstrated.
